Area.evidence_source: [page/6/Text/4] Prior to their attempt many participants felt they had lost control over important aspects of their lives and functioning, which seemed to signify an overall reduction in independence and autonomy. This was met with a desire to return to a previous state of equilibrium and a growing awareness that this was no longer possible as things were felt to be changing for the worse. Losses included those related to health, mobility, social status and social support, as well as those resulting from changing life circumstances. Some of the losses and changes were inextricably linked to the ageing process; others were sometimes unrelated to ageing but were experienced within the context of old age.[page/6/Text/7] As the suicide attempt drew closer, however, many attempts to maintain control proved ineffective. It is likely that the tension between losing control and trying to maintain it contributed to feelings of helplessness and depression.[page/6/Text/15] The attempt was construed by these individuals as a failure experience, a failure to problem-solve or regain some sort of control in a helpless situation. This generated feelings of shame that were often cloaked in humour:[page/6/Text/17] At the heart of this theme was a continued helplessness as the attempt appeared to have brought little change and no further control over life:[page/6/Text/19] In contrast, there was an optimism pervading the accounts of those participants who felt they had regained control over their life after the attempt. This was often associated with an alleviation of pain, physical health symptoms or even depression due to the medical care they received when hospitalised.
